body.text: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says an OpenAI agent accessed public and private data after hacking into a Medicare data portal in June.
Mr Albanese said the company took three months to admit the breach.

One of the first instances of AI agent attacking government infrastructure
Associate Professor on AI Governance at University of Queensland, Michael Noetel said it shows our government infrastructures aren’t ‘strong enough’ to protect against current AI models.

"The last six months we have seen an increasing number of AI models trying to solve problems and hacking other websites, breaking the law in the process, and so starting to attack Government infrastructure is showing how fragile our safeguards are,” he told ABC News Breakfast. "This is the first time I have seen an AI model attack Government infrastructure."

"The last six months we have seen an increasing number of AI models trying to solve problems and hacking other websites, breaking the law in the process, and so starting to attack Government infrastructure is showing how fragile our safeguards are,” he told ABC News Breakfast.
"This is the first time I have seen an AI model attack Government infrastructure."
The AI hack on Australian government sites was in June but wasn’t reported until recently.

"It shows that we are relying on the AI companies their goodwill and disclosure, not laws, that require them to disclose incidents. "Whereas if you look at more established industries like aviation, if there's a crash, there's a requirement we investigate it and report it and that isn't just that we get like Boeing decide whether or not they do that,” he said.
"It shows that we are relying on the AI companies their goodwill and disclosure, not laws, that require them to disclose incidents.

"Whereas if you look at more established industries like aviation, if there's a crash, there's a requirement we investigate it and report it and that isn't just that we get like Boeing decide whether or not they do that,” he said.
Mr Noetel highlighted the need for laws around the use of AI and oversight on the rapidly growing industry.
"It’s almost like there is a bus heading towards a cliff, we can’t just talk about seatbelts, we need the Government to stop the bus.”
Angus Taylor questions timing of AI hack announcement
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says the OpenAI hack is a "serious warning" about the security of government systems in a world of artificial intelligence.
He says the government needs to be transparent about the breach.
“When it first became aware of the breach, exactly what information was accessed, what vulnerability was exploited, how they’re closing it."
Mr Taylor says Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is not across the issue, accusing him of "failing to pre-empt" the incident.
He also questioned the timing of the prime minister's announcement.
“Why is he talking about it now when he’s over in the US? I mean this happened some time back. We’ve not heard him talking about these issues,” he said.
Has OpenAI broken any Australian laws? Marles is unsure
"That's a good question," Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles says.
Marles told ABC Radio National Breakfast the government has yet to determine whether OpenAI broke the law for the Medicare portal hack.

"That's one that we are working through here, and so we will look at what is the legal situation in respect of this, and what it means to have gained an unauthorised access, albeit in an unintended way. So that is one of the questions that we're continuing to investigate through the task force," he says.
Marles says that taskforce will look at why the breach had to be reported by OpenAI rather than Australia's security agencies.
But he stressed the data accessed by OpenAI on the portal was on the "lower end of sensitivity" and guarded by a digital "fence".
"I mean, we're not talking about the very highly sensitive information that we have in respect of national security," he says, arguing such data is kept behind a what he described as a "fortress".
Anthropic and OpenAI warned UN of artificial intelligence security risks
Yesterday, the United Nations Security Council was warned of the risks artificial intelligence poses to humanity by leading global AI companies.

Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei told the 15-member council he believed "AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole", appealing for governments to work together to manage the increasingly powerful technology.
Meanwhile, OpenAI boss Sam Altman said international cooperation was needed.

"If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people they serve," he told the UNSC.

The council was meeting as Prime Minister Anthony Albanese held a press conference in New York, revealing an OpenAI agent had infiltrated the Medicare services portal in June, accessing public and non-public files.
Key Event
Marles doesn't think there was 'a lot of data' involved in hack
Richard Marles is downplaying concerns about the size and scale of the Medicare portal hack.
The acting prime minister told ABC's Radio National Breakfast the impact was "relatively minor", but the government is taking the issue very seriously.

"I don't think we're talking about a lot of data in the sense that it was essentially asking a question and seeking specific answers. But to be clear, we are still investigating all of that and we are working with OpenAI in relation to it," he says.
Key Event
Full statement from OpenAI
We've just got our hands on a full statement from OpenAI regarding the Medicare portal hack.
Here's what a spokesperson for the company had to say:

"As we've shared publicly, OpenAI is conducting an extensive review of misaligned model activity during training and evaluation and notifying third parties when our review identifies potential impacts to their systems.

"During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation. In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend.

"Our review found no evidence of patient records being accessed. The information accessed included aggregate health statistics and internal file names. We notified the organisations and are providing technical information to support their investigations and help address potential security vulnerabilities. Our overall review is ongoing, and we remain committed to transparency about these issues and to sharing what we learn as that work continues."
What was Open AI trying to do?
Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles has been asked on Radio National Breakfast what led to the incident and whether the government had been told what happened.
He says OpenAI was working on developing "more sophisticated" artificial intelligence models.
In that context, an AI model was given a task to research health and medical statistics and, as a result, approached four Australian government websites.
One was the Victorian Department of Health, another was a New South Wales government website, and then there was the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.
In those cases, it just looked through information that was available to the public.
But Mr Marles said that was not the case with the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal.

"It sought information, information was not given, and then it effectively hacked into that medical portal and got that information anyway," he said. "And that's the unauthorised access, which we are very concerned about. "The information is benign in a sense and as I say, the impact is relatively minor, but the incident is very serious."
"It sought information, information was not given, and then it effectively hacked into that medical portal and got that information anyway," he said.
"And that's the unauthorised access, which we are very concerned about.
"The information is benign in a sense and as I say, the impact is relatively minor, but the incident is very serious."
Key Event
OpenAI says no evidence patient records accessed
News agency Reuters is reporting a statement from OpenAI about the Australian Medicare cyber hack.
The company says its AI agent improperly accessed files involving "several Australian government websites and services", but there is no evidence patient records were accessed.
"We weren't aware of agent activity in Australia until August during an ongoing review of OpenAI misaligned model activity," the statement from the company says.
OpenAI says it notified Services Australia — which administers the Medicare statistics service portal — about the incident on September 10.
'Lots of questions' to answer on cybersecurity, shadow health minister says
Shadow Health Minister Anne Ruston says she will be requesting a full government briefing on the extent of the impact on health services.
"We need to understand what our government systems are capable of defending, and we need to have a key audit of those government systems," the senator told ABC Radio National.
"The fact that this happened is serious enough, but the fact that we had to wait for OpenAi to notify the government is even more concerning."
Senator Ruston says it's concerning that it took three months for the hack to be identified.
"There are a lot of questions the government needs to answer."
Indo-Pacific not a 'chessboard', Albanese to say in key speech at UNGA

After signing the security pact with Ukraine, the prime minister will deliver a major foreign policy speech warning the US and China that the Indo-Pacific is not a "chessboard" for global superpowers.
The strategic competition between the two countries is the most "consequential factor" shaping our region, he will say.
"The Indo-Pacific is not a chessboard on which superpowers move the pieces," Mr Albanese will say (according to excerpts from his speech).
"How Washington and Beijing manage their relationship matters profoundly."
You can read more on this from our national affairs correspondent Jane Norman, who's in New York, in the story below.
Key Event
PM signs new security pact with Netherlands on sidelines of UNGA
Reporting by pool reporter Katina Curtis

Anthony Albanese and Netherlands Prime Minister Rob Jetten have signed a new strategic partnership covering cooperation on security and defence, economics and trade, climate, Ukraine, justice for the MH17 victims, and creative industries.
The two leaders met in the GAB-1 bilateral booth just outside the UN General Assembly chamber.
They signed the agreement documents after their talks.
"Australia and the Netherlands recognise the need to continue investing in our close cooperation to meet current and future challenges," the strategic partnership states.

Albanese, wearing his navy and cream "origami rabbit" tie, pointed to the Australian coat of arms on the front of his folder and told Jetten: "A little fun fact about Australia: our coat of arms, these two animals, can't go backwards. They can only go forward."
Jetten replied that that was the "spirit of the agreement".
The Netherlands coat of arms on Jetten’s folder depicted two lions.
Key Event
Timeline of who knew what and when
Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles has described the AI hack as a "very serious incident" and "completely unacceptable".
While the hack occurred in June, Mr Marles said the Australian government wasn't notified until months later.
"We became aware of this as government a couple of weeks ago," he told News Breakfast.

"Ministers were informed at the end of last week and over the weekend, and over the last few days we have been assuring ourselves of what the impact has been in relation to data and the portal itself and for what that's worth, that's relatively minor."
Mr Marles says a taskforce has now been established to investigate the incident.

"That will be led by the Prime Minister and Cabinet department, which will also work with the Australian Signals Directorate and the AI Safety Institute, to examine everything that's occurred here and to understand what the AI agent did and how this incursion occurred and what the impact of it has been," he said.
Medicare AI hac 'somewhat expected', says Greens senator
Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young says the government needs to put an immediate stop to the growth of AI in Australia following the hack.
"Australians are rightly worried and concerned about the power of this technology and the lack of regulation and lack of guardrails," she told News Breakfast.
"We know that it's a technology that is expanding rapidly ... we've got big AI like OpenAI – this exact company – in talks with governments to set up their big data facilities here in Australia.
"I urge the prime minister to not waste this moment. Big AI needs regulation. And it's not there yet. And we should put a pause, put a moratorium, before we let them run loose here in Australia.
She said news of the hack was "extraordinary, but somewhat expected".
The senator also questioned why it took OpenAI three months to alert the government about the incident.
PM's comments on hack into Medicare portal
Anthony Albanese delivered news of the OpenAI hack into Medicare at a press conference in New York, where the prime minister is currently attending the UN General Assembly.
He said there was no evidence any individual personal information had been accessed, but an investigation aided by the Australian Signals Directorate was now underway.

"Today I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, to express Australia's extreme concern about this incident," the PM said. "And I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred. "The nature of the way that the notification occurred as well was unacceptable."

"And I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred.
"The nature of the way that the notification occurred as well was unacceptable."
Good morning
Thanks for joining me on the blog this morning.
I'm Heloise Vyas, taking over the reins from my colleague Courtney Gould today, and I'll keep you across the political goings-on here and in New York, where the UN General Assembly continues.
But first, this morning we've heard that an OpenAI hack of an Australian Medicare portal earlier this year saw both public and private data exposed.
PM Anthony Albanese has called the incident "unacceptable" and said he had spoken with the company's CEO, Sam Altman.
We'll bring you more as we have it.
